sections.b: Ezekiel gives Egypt seven oracles in chapters 29 to 32, the longest series against any nation. Pharaoh is a great sea monster in the Nile (29:3), a reed staff that broke in Israel's hand (29:6-7), a tree cut down (31) and a young lion who is really a monster (32:2). Egypt will be empty for forty years, then brought back as a lowly kingdom (29:11-15). Nebuchadnezzar is given Egypt as wages for his work at Tyre (29:17-20). The oracles can be read beside Jeremiah 46 and Isaiah 19.

sections.h: The descent to Sheol in Ezekiel 31 and 32
sections.b: Ezekiel 31 and 32 give the fullest picture in the prophets of the dead as a company. The great tree goes down to Sheol and the Pit (31:15-18), and in 32:17-32 the nations lie in rows around their graves, killed by the sword and "uncircumcised," greeting the newcomer. Isaiah 14:9-11 has a related scene. The chapters are a satire on empire as much as a picture of the afterlife.

In April 571 BC Ezekiel says that Nebuchadnezzar and his army got no pay from the long siege of Tyre, so the LORD gives him Egypt as wages for work done for him (29:17-20). The text treats the king as a hired worker in God's service without naming him servant. Babylon's sword is again named against Egypt in 30:10-12 and 32:11. A Babylonian tablet tells of a campaign against Egypt in 568/567 BC.

Ezekiel uses "the uncircumcised" for the honorless dead in Sheol, those killed by the sword and laid without honor (28:10; 31:18; 32:19-32). Egypt's people practiced circumcision, as Herodotus notes, and Jeremiah lists Egypt with the nations that are "circumcised in a foreskin" (Jeremiah 9:25-26), so the word in Ezekiel is not a plain label for a foreign people.

The lament over Pharaoh (32:2-16) belongs with the dirges Ezekiel sings for Judah's kings (19), Tyre (27) and the king of Tyre (28:12-19). It is a funeral song for a king who is still alive. The second part (32:17-32) is a chant over the whole multitude.

sections.h: A Day of the LORD for Egypt
sections.b: Ezekiel 30:1-19 gives Egypt its own Day of the LORD, a day of cloud and a time for the nations, opened with the cry "Alas for the day." The same cry opens the Day in Joel 1:15, and Obadiah and Isaiah 13 speak of the Day against other nations.

sections.h: Pharaoh as the great sea monster
sections.b: Ezekiel 29:3 and 32:2 call Pharaoh the tannin, the great water monster, which Isaiah and the Psalms call a dragon. Ezekiel's picture is also of a Nile crocodile, caught with hooks and a net. The Greek translates it "dragon." In Isaiah 30:7 and Psalm 87:4 Egypt is called Rahab, another name for the chaos monster.

sections.h: The trees of Eden in Ezekiel 31
sections.b: In Ezekiel 31 the garden of God is a forest of trees that envy the great cedar and go down with it to the earth below. The same garden appears for the king of Tyre in 28:13 and for the restored land in 36:35.

Cush is the land south of Egypt. Ezekiel says anguish will fall on Cush when Egypt falls (30:4), that its people are among Egypt's soldiers (30:5), and that God's messengers go by ship to shake "carefree Cush" (30:9). The border of the ruin is "the border of Cush" (29:10).
Elam appears in Ezekiel only in the list of the dead in Sheol (32:24-25). Jeremiah has a longer word against it (Jeremiah 49:34-39).

After the short oracles against Ammon, Moab, Edom, Philistia, Tyre and Sidon (25 to 28), Ezekiel gives Egypt seven oracles in four chapters (29 to 32), with a lament and a chant of the nations in Sheol at the end. Babylon, the empire that carried out the judgments, gets no oracle.

sections.h: A prophecy corrected: Tyre and Egypt
sections.b: Ezekiel 26:7-14 foretold the plunder of Tyre by Nebuchadnezzar. In 29:17-20 the prophet says the army got no wages from Tyre and gives Egypt in its place. The book keeps both words. Readers take this as honesty, as revision, or as the same promise fulfilled another way.
